# Model Principles {.unnumbered}

The repair task begins with a model call that proposes an inspection or a patch. The call consumes resources even when its output is unusable, and a complete response still leaves the runtime to check what it proposes. Part I makes this boundary concrete. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model establishes what a request supplies, how the response reports completion, and how input and output contribute to cost. @Sec-vol3-test-time-compute then considers how longer generation, additional candidates, and feedback change the chance of obtaining a useful result within a fixed budget. Neither a more expensive call nor a larger collection of proposals grants authority to act.

A request can include a long source excerpt and ask for a short edit, or ask the model to reproduce the entire changed file. Those choices impose different amounts of input processing and output generation. Autoregressive output conditions each token on the preceding sequence; in the ordinary token-by-token implementation, each additional token adds another generation step. The time per step depends on the serving configuration, so the engineering rule concerns a measured cost rather than a universal ratio.

::: {#pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding .callout-principle title="Output-bound latency"}

**Invariant**: Under a fixed serving configuration with approximately stable generation time per token, output-generation latency grows approximately with output length. For unbatched dense-model decoding whose weight reads dominate, memory bandwidth supplies a lower bound on that step time. This bound does not describe every serving configuration or the whole call's latency.

**Implication**: When generation dominates the call, an interface that expresses the same useful proposal in fewer tokens can reduce latency. Input processing, queueing, and checks must still fit the task's deadline. Compare interfaces at a matched task budget rather than assuming that shorter output is always better. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost prices a concrete call; @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline derives the hardware estimate and its assumptions.

:::

The runtime must also distinguish time spent from work completed. A call interrupted by a limit, a cancellation, or a lost connection may leave a partial payload, even if that payload parses. Completion status therefore precedes handling the output as a finished candidate. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract develops this gate without treating a completed generation as evidence that the task succeeded. Additional inference then raises two separate questions: whether a useful candidate is available and whether the system can identify it.

::: {#pri-vol3-test-time-scaling .callout-principle title="Evidence-bounded deliberation"}

**Invariant**: Producing a valid candidate and selecting a valid candidate are different events. Additional sampling can increase the chance that a candidate set contains a useful result; that increase alone does not establish which result should be accepted. The reliability of the selected result depends on the generation process, the selection rule, and the evidence available to that rule.

**Implication**: Allocate a task's budget across generation, candidate assessment, and feedback, and measure the outcome of the complete policy. Compare against a single-candidate baseline under the same limits, including unsuccessful attempts and checks in the cost. Stop or escalate when the remaining budget cannot support the required evidence, rather than treating more generated text as evidence by itself.

:::

For the repair, generating several patches may expose alternatives that one call missed. A compiler can reject some of them, and a regression test can distinguish others. Neither check establishes every property of the intended repair. Selection can exploit a weak check as well as a useful one, making the scope of the check part of the design.

::: {#pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry .callout-principle title="The verification asymmetry"}

**Invariant**: Checking a stated property and establishing that the property captures the task are different obligations. A checker can be exact for a specified property under explicit assumptions, while tests and judgments provide evidence with limited coverage. Repeatable verdicts and protection from modification do not, by themselves, establish task-level correctness.

**Implication**: State what each check supports, protect its criteria and observations from the actions it judges, and preserve unresolved requirements in the acceptance decision. Learned assessments can help rank or revise candidates, but do not supply permission to act or an independent guarantee of correctness. Acceptance applies the task contract's evidence standard; insufficient evidence calls for an unresolved outcome or escalation.

:::

These principles connect the price of a call to the responsibility for its result. The runtime bounds generation and handles incomplete responses, while candidate selection uses evidence whose limits remain explicit. The invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) continues to govern both responsibilities. Part I supplies a usable model-call contract and a way to assess additional inference; the later parts supply the state, tools, and execution control needed to carry those decisions through a trajectory.
